title: Tractable probability without polynomial-size deterministic decomposable lineage
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal:
Does there exist a finite relational signature \(\sigma\) and a fixed Boolean union of conjunctive queries \(q\) over \(\sigma\) with both following properties?

First, a deterministic Turing machine computes the exact probability \(\Pr[q(I_p)]\) in time polynomial in the entire binary input length, for every finite explicitly given database \(I\) and every assignment of rational inclusion probabilities \(p_t\in[0,1]\) to its facts \(t\in I\), retained independently in \(I_p\).

Second, the lineage functions have no polynomial size bound in deterministic decomposable Boolean circuits with arbitrary internal negations:
\[
\forall C,c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists I:\quad
\operatorname{ddsize}(\operatorname{Lin}(q,I))>C\bigl(N(I)+1\bigr)^c.
\]
Here \(N(I)\) is the unweighted database encoding length and the circuit model is defined below. The query and signature are fixed before all databases and probability assignments; no unproved complexity assumption is part of the question.
why: Probability evaluation can combine numerical cancellations that may not correspond to a small reusable Boolean explanation. A separation would show that efficient numerical inference is strictly more general than the existence of compact deterministic decomposable lineage.

sentences: The query is a fixed Boolean union of conjunctive queries on a tuple-independent probabilistic database.
The question asks whether its exact probability can be computed in polynomial bit time while its Boolean lineage has no polynomial-size deterministic decomposable circuit.
The circuit may use negation at any depth and need not be constructible efficiently.
A known compilation result eliminates a former candidate and covers a substantial special family.
A recent obstruction to one proposed construction method does not yet establish the required general separation.

definitions:
A signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each of a fixed positive integer arity. A database consists of a finite explicitly listed domain, identified with \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a set of distinct ground facts for each relation. Domain elements and tuple coordinates are encoded in binary with delimiters; the domain list is explicit. The empty domain is permitted. The unweighted encoding length \(N(I)\) includes the domain, relation tags and all tuples, but not the probabilities. Choosing another ordinary explicit encoding with polynomially related lengths gives the same size question.

A Boolean union of conjunctive queries is a finite disjunction of sentences \(\exists x_1\cdots\exists x_k\,\bigwedge_j R_j(\bar x_j)\). Every variable occurs in an atom, repeated variables and repeated relation symbols are allowed, and there are no free variables, function symbols, order predicates, inequalities or negated atoms. Variables range over the supplied domain. The query is true when at least one disjunct has an assignment making all its atoms facts of the database. Equality constraints can be eliminated by identifying variables; they add no expressive power here. The query and signature are not inputs to the probability algorithm.

An input probability is a binary numerator and positive binary denominator specifying a rational in \([0,1]\), including the endpoints. The weighted input length includes all these integers. The required output is a binary rational numerator and denominator for
\[
\sum_{J\subseteq I:\ J\models q}\ \prod_{t\in J}p_t\prod_{t\in I\setminus J}(1-p_t).
\]
Each subdatabase has the same supplied domain. Running time counts bit operations, including writing the exact output. Constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on the fixed query. There is no promise restricting probabilities or database structure.

For each fact \(t\in I\) introduce a Boolean input variable \(X_t\). The lineage \(\operatorname{Lin}(q,I)\) maps an assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\) to one exactly when the subdatabase \(\{t:x_t=1\}\) satisfies \(q\). Thus it is independent of the chosen probabilities.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output, constant gates zero and one, a single available input gate for each fact variable used, AND and OR gates of fan-in two, and NOT gates of fan-in one. Fan-out is unrestricted. Its size is the number of vertices plus edges. No auxiliary input variables, quantifiers, oracle gates or probability-dependent operations are allowed. Unused fact variables need not be present. The variable set of a gate is the set of input labels having a directed path to it. At every AND gate, the two input subcircuits must have disjoint variable sets. At every OR gate, there must be no Boolean assignment making both input subcircuits true. NOT gates may take any gate as input, at any depth. In particular, negations are not restricted to literals, and no common variable tree or decision diagram structure is imposed. These are deterministic decomposable circuits, often denoted d-D or d-DNNF with internal negation allowed.

The quantity \(\operatorname{ddsize}(F)\) is the minimum size of such a circuit computing \(F\) on every assignment. A finite circuit always exists, for example a disjunction of the disjoint full assignments accepted by \(F\). The size assertion concerns existence of representations, not the complexity of constructing them: each circuit may depend arbitrarily on its whole unweighted database. Refuting the displayed separation means proving that every fixed query with the stipulated polynomial probability algorithm has some polynomial lineage size bound, with constants allowed to depend on that query. It does not require a polynomial-time compiler.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence statement. A positive answer must exhibit a fixed Boolean UCQ, prove its uniform exact polynomial-bit-time probability algorithm, and prove the absence of every polynomial d-D lineage size bound. A lower bound only for negation-normal-form, structured or decision circuits does not suffice. A negative answer must establish polynomial d-D size for every query meeting the probability premise; an efficient circuit-construction algorithm is not additionally required.

source_formulation.text: The author asks for a Boolean UCQ whose probabilities are computable in polynomial time but whose lineage needs superpolynomial deterministic decomposable circuits, expressly allowing internal negation. The card specifies rational input encodings and the existential size quantifiers without replacing the circuit class by a restricted subclass.

context_blocks.text: The representation model allows complements of whole subcircuits. Lower bounds for ordinary negation-normal-form representations therefore do not settle this question.
Monet constructs suitable circuits for an important safe query family, including the former candidate q9. This eliminates that candidate without establishing compilation for all tractable UCQs.

The August 2026 preprint refutes a combinatorial conjecture used in one proposed construction route. Failure of that route does not itself prove a lower bound against all deterministic decomposable circuits.
